change.excerpt: Gradivus knew that this was a signal given to him for the promised removal; and, leaning on his lance, he boldly mounted {behind} his steeds, laden with the blood-stained pole {of the chariot}, and urged them on with the lash of the whip; and descending along the steep air, he stood on the summit of the hill of the woody Palatium; and he took away the son of Ilia, that moment giving out his royal ordinances to his own Quirites. His mortal body glided through the yielding air; just as the leaden plummet, discharged from the broad sling, is wont to dissolve itself[62] in mid air. A beauteous appearance succeeded, one more suitable to the lofty couches[63] of heaven, and a form, such as that of Quirinus arrayed in his regal robe.

narrativeBlocks.title: Romulus after the conflict
narrativeBlocks.body: After the Romans and Sabines agree to share rule, Ovid turns to Romulus's divine future. Mars, named Mavors in Riley's translation, asks Jupiter to honor his grandson.

narrativeBlocks.title: Mars makes the request
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Riley's translation; whitespace normalized): “The time is {now} come, O father, (since the Roman state is established on a strong foundation, and is no longer dependent on the guardianship of but one), for thee to give the reward which was promised to me, and to thy grandson {so} deserving of it, and, removed from earth, to admit him to heaven.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Romulus becomes Quirinus
narrativeBlocks.body: Jupiter assents, and Romulus is taken from earth to heaven. Ovid describes a new appearance and names the deified founder Quirinus.

narrativeBlocks.title: A Roman foundation narrative
narrativeBlocks.body: This is Ovid's epic account of Rome's legendary founder and divine status, not independent historical evidence that the events occurred.

narrativeBlocks.title: Warrior ancestry and civic identity
narrativeBlocks.body: The poem links Mars, Romulus, and the Roman state through an act of literary apotheosis: a mortal founder becomes a deity in Ovid's narrative.
